transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Russia and Ukraine continue to attack each other as the Trump administration pushes for a new round of peace talks.
Local officials say strikes from the Kremlin killed 10 people and injured 40 others.
Ukraine launched a drone attack overnight at Russian targets.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports Russian forces targeted Ukrainian power grids and warehouses.
U.S. Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner flew to Moscow to meet with President Vladimir Putin
and then saw Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky Thursday night in Dublin.
We just had talks with our American partners.
Standing beside the U.S. Envoy Zelensky said he hoped each meeting would bring them closer to peace.
Zelensky hailed the agreement for a massive prisoner exchange and the fact that Kushner says the Europeans will now be at the table.
They will have a voice. It's important for us because the war is in Europe.
But Putin has not backed off any of his hard-line positions and says any European peacekeepers in Ukraine would be considered a legitimate target.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Kyiv.
A leadership race is taking shape among Senate Democrats as the party prepares to take control of the chamber in January.
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is challenging Chuck Schumer for the role of majority leader.
Van Hollen says the outcome of the midterm election should serve as a guide for the party moving forward.
This is not about any one individual, but it is about answering the call of the American people.
We saw a huge outburst of democracy on election day, red states, blue states, purple states, and it wasn't only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption and his wars and his cruelty.
It was also about a call for a larger change.
Schumer is seeking to retain his position as the party's leader in the Senate.
Nearly two dozen states, mostly led by Republicans, are contributing National Guard troops to President Trump's military deployment in Washington, D.C.
NPR's Kat Lonsdorf reports newly elected Democratic governors are facing growing pressure to bring those troops home when they take office next year.
Voters in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Texas, and Ohio flipped their governors to Democrats in last week's midterms.
All five of those states are currently sending troops to Washington.
Georgia has the largest presence of any state, with more than 500 in the city.
They're part of President Trump's ongoing and controversial deployment, which started in August of last year and has thousands of armed service members patrolling streets in an effort to fight crime, which was already at a 30-year low before the deployment.
Members of the D.C. Council are calling on the newly elected Democratic governors to commit to pulling their troops once in office.
NPR reached out to all five governors-elect, but did not receive a response.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Washington.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The World Health Organization says tuberculosis remains the leading cause of death from infectious disease globally, though not in the U.S.
NPR's Jonathan Lambert says overall deaths from TB have declined 35 percent over the past decade.
TB is a preventable disease that can usually be cured, but because of limited access to testing and adequate treatment, more than 10 million people get sick each year and about 1 million die.
But over the past decade, efforts to expand testing and treatment have helped prevent hundreds of thousands of deaths, according to the WHO report.
But this progress is threatened by cuts to international aid, which fell by 14 percent from 2024 to 2025.
While domestic spending ticked up, overall funding levels are still several billion dollars below targets.
TB is a slow-moving disease, and the report author suggests that it's too soon to see the impact of aid cuts in official data.
But they warned that progress could slip if countries don't have the funds to maintain testing and treatment.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
The U.S. men's national soccer team is losing its head coach.
Mauricio Pochettino is leaving to take over as manager of Manchester United.
He led the U.S. to the knockout stage of this year's World Cup and signed a four-year contract extension in August.
Pochettino will coach the Americans in two upcoming matches against Haiti before taking over the English club.
Stocks are trading lower on Wall Street at the sour.
The Dow was down 131 points.
The Nasdaq composite down 474.
I'm Windsor Johnston, NPR News, in Washington.

Senator Chris Van Hollen challenges Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leadership

Newly elected Democratic governors face pressure to pull National Guard troops from Washington
WHO report says tuberculosis deaths fell 35 percent over decade, but aid cuts threaten progress
Mauricio Pochettino leaves U.S. men's soccer team to manage Manchester United
Stocks trade lower on Wall Street, with Dow and Nasdaq both falling
